rashi:a1.1: He gave four for the first: that is, the priest valuated him for the first vow first. He has not fulfilled the first, since he must give all that he has, in accordance with the Rabbis. And if he later became wealthy, he gives the entire valuation, since the first giving counts for nothing.
rashi:a2.1: All of them are fit for this one, etc.: and one of the valuations still remains upon him.
rashi:a4.1: But more than a sela there is: even though he does not have fifty sela; for if he had five sela in his possession he gives all of them, which is more than a sela and less than fifty. And the unattributed mishna is in accordance with the Rabbis, since according to Rabbi Meir there is no [payment by the] means [of the vower] that comes to more than a sela and less than fifty for one whose valuation is fifty; [it is either fifty] or a sela.
rashi:a5.1: Mishna. Petaḥ: the beginning of niddah [the opening of a menstrual period]. For this is the Torah law of a niddah: if she saw [blood] today, she counts six and it [i.e., today, seven in all]; if she saw two days, she counts five and them; and even if she saw all seven and it stopped by evening, she immerses and may engage in relations. From the seventh day on are the eleven days of ziva: if she sees on them one day or two, she keeps a day for a day [one clean day for each] and immerses; and if she sees on them three consecutive days, she is a full zava and requires a count of seven clean days and an offering. And if her days of flow extend for a month or a year, she does not return to the beginning of niddah until she sits seven clean days; once she has sat seven clean days and then sees, it is the beginning of niddah, and she counts six and it, and returns to her course, all as explained. And if she did not see three consecutive days during those eleven days, she is not a zava, and when she sees afterward, whether soon after or later, it is the beginning of niddah; and even if she then sees three consecutive days, she counts only four and them, since the days of flow are only those eleven days between the end of this niddah and the beginning of the next. And so it is explained in the last halakha of tractate Niddah (72a).
rashi:a5.2: There is no petaḥ for a to’ah [a woman who has lost count] in fewer than seven: a to’ah who saw [blood] today and does not know whether she stands in her days of niddah or in those eleven days of ziva does not return to the opening of her niddah in fewer than seven clean days.
rashi:a5.3: And not more than seventeen: clean days, as is explained in the Gemara.
rashi:a6.1: Gemara. The Sages taught: a to’ah who said, I saw one impure day: today, and she does not know whether it is in the days of the beginning of niddah, so that she must count six and it, or in those eleven days of flow, so that she need keep only a day for a day.
rashi:a6.2: Her petaḥ is seventeen: if she does not see until after seventeen [days], apart from this day, she returns to the opening of her niddah, to count six and it. For whichever way you look at it, after seventeen apart from this day she has left the doubt of the days of flow. If this day on which she saw was at the beginning of the days of ziva, once the eleven days are over she has left the days of flow, and since her next seeing was far off, not until after seventeen, it is the beginning of niddah. And even if you say this day was the beginning of niddah, she has nevertheless left the days of flow, for six have passed to complete her days of niddah and the eleven that are between niddah and niddah, which is seventeen; so after seventeen, when she sees, it is the beginning of niddah. But if she sees on the seventeenth day, she has not left the doubt whether it is a day of niddah or a day of ziva: perhaps the day on which she came before us was the first of the days of niddah, and the seventeenth day on which she saw is the end of the eleven days between niddah and niddah, so that she needs only to keep [a day for a day]; or perhaps the first day on which she came before us was of the days of ziva, and when the eleven days ended she left the days of flow, and the seventeenth day on which she saw is the beginning of niddah, so that she must count six and it. And all the more so if she sees before seventeen. In this doubt she remains indefinitely until she sits seventeen clean days. And all the while she is in this doubt she is badly disordered, for we always act stringently with her: when she sees one day within these seventeen days, we say it is the beginning of niddah and she needs six and it; and when she sees three consecutive days, we say they are days of flow and she needs seven clean days and an offering out of doubt, and it is not eaten. But after seventeen there is no call for stringency, for it is certainly the beginning of niddah: if she sees three consecutive days she counts four and them, and after the seven, if she sees, she keeps a day for a day, and on the third day she is a zava.
rashi:a7.1: Two impure days I saw, her petaḥ is seventeen: apart from these two days. For if she does not see until after seventeen, it is the beginning of niddah whichever way you look at it. If these two days were of the days of flow, the days of flow ended nine days after the two, and since her seeing was far off, at the end of seventeen, it is the beginning of niddah. And if it was the beginning of niddah, the days of niddah and flow ended sixteen days after the two, since the days of niddah and flow are only eighteen; so this one who did not see until after seventeen, which is the twentieth day from the beginning of the doubtful seeing, is a niddah. But if she sees on the seventeenth day, and all the more so before that, she has not left the doubt: perhaps these two days were the beginning of niddah, and sixteen days after the two the days of niddah and flow ended, and this seeing on the seventeenth day is the beginning of niddah; or perhaps one of the two days was the end of the eleven of ziva and the second the beginning of niddah, and the days of niddah and ziva did not end until after seventeen, and this seeing on the seventeenth day is the end of ziva. So she is in doubt. And all the more so if she sees earlier, for example on the thirteenth and fourteenth day, she stands in doubt: perhaps these two days on which she came before us were the end of the days of flow, and this one who did not see again until the thirteenth day is at the beginning of niddah; or perhaps the two days were the beginning of niddah, and this thirteenth day is the eighth of the days of flow, and she keeps a day for a day. And so she remains in this doubt indefinitely until she sits seventeen clean days.
rashi:a8.1: Three impure days I saw, her petaḥ is seventeen: as I explained. But before that, for example on the seventeenth itself, she stands in doubt, and one may say: perhaps two of the three days were the end of ziva and the third the beginning of niddah, and this seventeenth day is the end of ziva; or perhaps all three were the beginning of niddah, and fifteen days after the three the days of niddah and flow ended, and this seventeenth day is the beginning of niddah. But on the eighteenth day she has left the doubt whichever way you look at it.
rashi:a9.1: Four days, etc., her petaḥ is sixteen: for if she does not see until after sixteen apart from these, she has left the doubt whichever way you look at it. If they were the beginning of niddah, the days of niddah and flow ended fourteen days after these four; if they were days of flow, all the more so they ended before sixteen, and now it is the beginning of niddah; and if you say two of them were the end of ziva and two the beginning of niddah, even so the days of niddah and flow ended at the end of sixteen. And one cannot say that perhaps three were the end of ziva and the fourth the beginning of niddah, so that they did not end until the end of seventeen: for if the three were the end of ziva, then when she saw on the fourth it is not the beginning of niddah. Once she has seen three consecutive days in the days of ziva she is a zava, and she never leaves the state of ziva to be at the beginning of niddah until she sits seven clean days, as it is written: “But if she be cleansed of her issue, then she shall number to herself seven days” (Leviticus 15:28); after she has sat seven clean days she returns to the beginning of her niddah. But if she sees before that, even on the sixteenth day, there is room for doubt between the end of ziva and the beginning of niddah: perhaps two of the four were the end of ziva and two the beginning of niddah, and the sixteenth day is the end of ziva; or perhaps the four were the beginning of niddah, or the end of ziva, and she has already left the days of niddah and flow.
rashi:a10.1: Five impure days I saw, her petaḥ is fifteen: whichever way you look at it, after fifteen it is the beginning of niddah if she sees. But if she sees on the fifteenth day itself it is a doubt, for perhaps two of the five were the end of ziva and the three were days of niddah, and this fifteenth day is still the end of the days of flow. And so throughout the baraita we take into account the doubt that the first two were the end of ziva and the later ones of niddah, but no more than that: for if you say three of them were the end of ziva, then the others would not be days of niddah so long as she has not sat seven clean days; and when she sees after sitting the seven clean days, it is the beginning of niddah.
tosafot:a2.1: Since he vowed both simultaneously, they take effect together: therefore, when the priest comes to valuate him, one may say he gives two and a half to this vow and likewise to the other. Or perhaps all of them are fit [for each], and the priest may only tell him to pay all five sela for one vow, since they were liened to one and not to two; and if he gives two and a half to this one and two and a half to that one, he has not fulfilled either, since the law is that he gives them to one alone. So at the moment he gives the five to both, all are liened to one, and it is like one who gave four to the first. And one must say that the case is where the priest valuates him for both together; for if one after the other, it would be no worse than one who gave to the second and then gave for the first, since certainly the creditors are equal, and what was collected is no worse than if it had been the later one [whose collection stands].
tosafot:a6.1: Her petaḥ is seventeen: that is, seventeen pure days. If she sees on the eighteenth, she is certainly a niddah; but if she sees on the seventeenth, perhaps it is a zava’s seeing, since the day on which she saw was the beginning of niddah, and the seventeenth day is the last day of the eleven days of ziva.
tosafot:a8.1: Three impure days: perhaps the first two days are of the eleven days and the third day is the first of niddah; therefore she needs seventeen. Four days, her petaḥ is sixteen, whichever way you look at it: for if we say the first three days are of the eleven [and she is a zava], then once her seven days of counting have passed she comes to the opening of her niddah. One cannot say that the last of the four days began her niddah, as that is impossible: since she is a major zava, she will never be a niddah until after counting seven days, the days of purity from ziva. Therefore the opening of her niddah can only be found by saying that perhaps the first two were of the days of ziva and her niddah did not begin until the third day, so that two days of her niddah have passed; and when five more days complete her niddah, and another eleven, which is sixteen days, you will find the opening of her niddah.
gershom:a1.1: He has not fulfilled the first: since all of them were liened to the first. He has fulfilled the second: since he had nothing more.
gershom:a2.1: Or perhaps all are fit for this one: [for this] valuation.
gershom:a3.1: And all are fit for that one: [for that] valuation, and he has not fulfilled both of them.
gershom:a4.1: But more than a sela there is, and less than fifty there is: that is, he gives what he has. And this is an unattributed statement in accordance with the Rabbis, who say he gives all of them.
gershom:a5.1: There is no petaḥ for a to’ah in fewer than seven, nor more than seventeen: that is, a woman who saw blood and is mistaken [to’ah], not knowing whether she is within the seven days of her niddah or within the eleven days of her ziva. For there are eleven days between niddah and niddah, on which she is either one who keeps a day for a day or a full zava: when she sees on them three consecutive days she is a full zava and needs seven clean days and an offering; but if she sees on them only one day, she keeps one clean day after it corresponding to it, immerses in the evening and is pure; and even if she saw two days, although she is a minor zava, she keeps the third day after them and immerses on the evening of the third. But a woman who is certainly a niddah is permitted after seven: if she saw blood on the first day, she counts six and it; likewise if she saw two days, she counts five and them; and likewise even if she saw six, she counts one and them, and is pure. And from the eighth until the eighteenth are eleven days under the law of ziva, as we explained. From the eighteenth on the days of ziva have stopped and the days of niddah return. But if she saw three days at the end of the eleven, she counts seven clean days after them, even outside the eleven days, from the eighteenth on. But when she is a to’ah, who saw and does not know whether she is within her days of niddah or her days of ziva, she never leaves her doubt to return to the certain opening of her niddah until she has ceased [bleeding] for seven clean days; that is the least measure she has. And her doubt does not extend beyond seventeen days, for after she has ceased for seventeen clean days she returns to her first permitted state, the certain opening of niddah. Then it explains how: a to’ah who said, I saw one impure day, and does not know whether it is in her days of niddah or her days of ziva, her petaḥ is seventeen: she does not return to the certain opening of her niddah until she has ceased for seventeen clean days. [And so] she needs seventeen because throughout this baraita we go stringently [and not leniently]. We say: perhaps that impure day was the beginning of her niddah, and she counts after it six days and the eleven full days of ziva, which is seventeen days, and after that she returns to the certain opening of her niddah. If you say that perhaps that impure day was the end of her ziva, she would need to cease for only seven clean days, as the law of a zava, and no more, and that is a leniency; and if you say that day was the beginning of ziva, she would need to cease for only one day, which is a greater leniency. Therefore we treat the doubt as the beginning of niddah, giving her the larger [measure], stringently. [The printed text repeats a line here by error; it is not translated.]
gershom:a6.1: Two impure days I saw, her petaḥ is seventeen: for we say perhaps the first was [the end of] the eleven of ziva and the other the beginning of niddah, so she must cease for six of niddah and the eleven of ziva, which is seventeen. If you say the reverse, she would need to keep only one day, which is a leniency.
gershom:a7.1: Three impure days I saw, her petaḥ is seventeen: for we say perhaps two were of the end of the eleven days of ziva and the third of the beginning of niddah, and she needs six and eleven, as we said. If you say the reverse, it is a leniency.
gershom:a8.1: Four impure days I saw, her petaḥ is sixteen: for we say the first two are of the end of the days of ziva and the last two of the beginning of niddah; five days of niddah remain, and eleven, which is sixteen. If the reverse, it is a leniency.
gershom:a9.1: Five impure days I saw, her petaḥ is fifteen: for we say the first two are of the end of ziva and three of the beginning of the days of niddah; four of niddah remain and eleven of ziva, so her petaḥ is fifteen. And so for all of them we say: perhaps the first two are of the end of the days of ziva, when she is one who keeps a day for a day, and the others of the beginning of the days of niddah; and whatever remains of the days of niddah is counted as clean days together with the eleven of ziva. Accordingly her petaḥ is fifteen.
gershom:a10.1: Nine impure days I saw, her petaḥ is eleven: for when you count the first two as the end of ziva and seven of niddah, only the eleven days of ziva remain.
gershom:a11.1: Ten impure days I saw, her petaḥ is ten: two of the end of ziva, seven of niddah, and one of the beginning of [the days of] ziva; ten of the days of ziva remain. And even though there are now three days of ziva, two before niddah and one after it, they do not combine to make her a full zava, so that her offering would be eaten, unless she is a zava for three consecutive days, either three before the days of niddah or three after the days of niddah; for those first eleven days of ziva do not combine with the other eleven days of ziva to make her a full zava.
gershom:a12.1: And likewise, I saw eleven impure [days], her petaḥ is nine: for we count the first two as the end of ziva, seven of niddah, and two of the beginning of ziva; that is “I saw eleven impure days.” Those of the end of ziva do not combine with those of the beginning of ziva to make her a full zava. Her petaḥ is nine, since that is what remains of the days of ziva.
gershom:b1.1: I saw twelve impure days: then she is a full zava, so that her offering is eaten, for we count the first two as the end of ziva, seven of niddah and three of ziva; now she is a full zava.
gershom:b2.1: Her petaḥ is eight: since that is what remains of the days of ziva. And all the more so one who says, I saw thirteen impure days, is a full zava, for whether before the seven days of niddah or after them there is enough to make her a full zava; and her petaḥ is seven, for when you add four of these last days to the seven days of niddah, making eleven, seven remain. And that is why it says: “There is no petaḥ for a to’ah in fewer than seven, etc.,” for after she ceases for these seven days she returns to the certain opening of her niddah: if she sees one day, she counts six and it and is certainly pure, as it is written: “She shall be in her impurity seven days” (Leviticus 15:19), and no more.
gershom:b3.1: Let her count seven clean days and be permitted to her husband: whichever way you look at it, for even if she is a full zava she needs only seven clean days and no more, as it is written: “But if she be cleansed of her issue” (Leviticus 15:28).
gershom:b4.1: We are speaking of setting her right as to niddah and its petaḥ: that is, all that we have said is in order to set her right, so that she returns to the certain opening of her niddah, so that in her days of niddah she need count only [five or four and them], and even if she saw six, she counts one and them and becomes pure; and so that she knows when she is a zava who is obligated in an offering.
gershom:b5.1: All the to’ot are zavot: every woman who saw blood and does not know whether it is in the days of niddah or the days of ziva is presumed a zava, for we go stringently. And the Talmud responds in astonishment: all to’ot are zavot? [How can it call them full zavot?] They are only possibly [full] zavot, possibly niddot.
gershom:b6.1: And furthermore, “I saw one impure day,” “I saw two impure days”: is she one who brings an offering? They are only in doubt, either possibly niddot or possibly one who keeps a day for a day, who does not bring an offering until she has seen three days; and she would be bringing non-sacred [animals] into the Temple courtyard.
gershom:b7.1: Rather, say: all zavot who are to’ot: [that is, from “I saw three impure days” on, where she is possibly a full zava, possibly a niddah, they bring an offering because of the possibility of ziva].
gershom:b8.1: And it is not eaten: as it is taught [in Nazir 29a]: Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda says: A provisional guilt offering is eaten; a bird sin offering brought for a doubt is not eaten. What is the reason? Here there is one doubt and there two doubts. A provisional guilt offering has only one doubt, possibly sacred, possibly non-sacred brought into the courtyard, and therefore it is eaten; it is eaten also because we say a person may volunteer [and bring] a provisional guilt offering every day, for if it does not come for this sin it comes for another. But a bird sin offering has two doubts of prohibition: possibly non-sacred in the courtyard, and possibly the prohibition of a carcass [since it requires pinching (melika), and if it is non-sacred it carries the prohibition of a carcass]. Therefore she brings an offering and it is not eaten.
gershom:b9.1: [Except for “her petaḥ is seven” and “her petaḥ is eight,” where she saw twelve days or thirteen days, for there no doubt can be raised: there she is certainly a full zava, as we said above. Therefore they bring an offering and it is eaten. As for those of whom they said, “they bring an offering and it is not eaten,” it goes either to burial or to burning.] (An editor’s gloss here says the meaning must be that it may not be left as it is, out of disrespect for consecrated food, and refers to the dispute in the mishna at Temura 34a.)
gershom:b10.1: There are no leprous marks less than one week [nor more than three weeks]: boils and burns are quarantined for one week, and houses are quarantined for three weeks; [this is explained in Torat Kohanim].
gershom:b11.1: “Your benevolence is like the mighty mountains”: leprous marks of a person, for the Holy One, Blessed be He, did him a kindness, that his quarantine is only one week.
gershom:b12.1: “Your judgments are like the great deep”: these are leprous marks of houses, whose judgment is not completed until three weeks.
gershom:b13.1: If not for Your benevolence: which is [great] like the mighty mountains, in that He hides away: when a person has half sins and half merits, He lifts one sin from the pan of the scales, removes it and forgives it, so that the merits outweigh.
gershom:b14.1: For if not so, if He did not take a sin from the pan, hide it away and store it if he does not sin [again], removing the first ones one by one, but let the [debits] outweigh, who could stand before Your judgments, [which sink] down to the great deep?
gershom:b15.1: Rava [the daf reads Rabba] says: “Your benevolence is like the mighty mountains”: in that You take a sin from the pan [and hide it] and store it; if he does not sin again You forgive him, and if he sinned, You join it with the other sins and judge him; because “Your judgments are like the great deep” for one who does not repent.
gershom:b16.1: Rava [the daf reads Rabba] is in accordance with Rabbi Elazar, who said “He hides away,” as we said. And there is a dispute about this [the text here is unclear] in tractate Rosh HaShana. (An editor’s gloss notes that Rosh HaShana cites only the dispute of Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Yosei bar Ḥanina, and suggests reading: “and the dispute of these Amoraim is in Rosh HaShana 17[a].”)
gershom:b17.1: [No fewer than four full months: of thirty days each. And (Ulla) [Rav Huna] explains in the Gemara why it did not seem right to the Sages to make more than eight full.]
rashi:b1.1: Twelve, her petaḥ is eight: for after she sits eight clean days she has left the doubt whichever way you look at it. Even if you say the first two were the end of ziva, eighteen days have been completed by the last count, the days of niddah and flow are over, and it is the beginning of niddah. But the eighth day itself is a doubt, for one may say: two of the twelve were the end of ziva, and of the ten, seven were niddah and three flow, so she is a zava; she has sat seven clean days, and this eighth day on which she saw is still within the eleven and is not the beginning of niddah, since there are not fewer than eleven days between the end of niddah and the beginning of niddah, and the twelve days by the last count have been completed. Or perhaps it is the beginning of niddah: the first of the twelve days was the beginning of niddah, and at the end of seven the days of niddah ended and on the eighth the days of ziva began, and by the twelfth day five of the days of flow had gone; so the days of flow end after six more, and after six the days of niddah and flow are over, and she has sat [seven] clean days for the ziva, so this eighth day is the beginning of niddah. That is a doubt and a great disorder, for she will not return to the opening of her niddah until after seventeen days, since she becomes again a to’ah who said, “I saw one impure day and I do not know whether it was in the days of niddah or the days of ziva.” If, after seeing on this eighth day, she ceases for seven days and then sees, and wishes to keep a day for a day, we are stringent with her and say: perhaps the day on which she saw was the end of ziva, and now it is the beginning of niddah. Or if she sees three days and wishes to count four days [to complete seven], we are stringent with her and say: perhaps that eighth day on which she saw was the beginning of niddah, and now she is in the days of flow and is a zava. And so she is in this doubt indefinitely, until she sits seven clean days.
rashi:b2.1: Thirteen, her petaḥ is seven: we take into account that the first two days were the end of ziva; eleven remain, and seven clean, which is eighteen.
rashi:b3.1: For there is no petaḥ for a to’ah in fewer than seven: for even if she saw fourteen, she does not return to her petaḥ in fewer than seven clean days, since whichever way you look at it she is a zava, and so long as she has not sat seven clean days she does not leave the state of ziva.
rashi:b4.1: Rav Adda said to him, etc.: Rav Adda erred, and thought that all these seventeen, sixteen and fifteen were stated in order to permit her to her husband.
rashi:b5.1: Niddah and its petaḥ: so that she knows from when she counts days of niddah. For [after this] if she sees three or four days, she counts only three and them [to complete seven], and the rest will be her days of flow, so that if she sees afterward she keeps a day [for a day].
rashi:b6.1: All to’ot are zavot: below he turns it around and explains, “Rather, all zavot who are to’ot,” that is, all those among the cases above whom we can treat as possibly zavot, which is all of them except “one impure day” and “two impure days,” since with fewer than three impure days she cannot possibly be a zava.
rashi:b6.2: They bring an offering: at the end of seven clean days, two turtledoves, one as a sin offering and one as a burnt offering, as the law of a zava, since perhaps they were zavot.
rashi:b6.3: And it is not eaten: the sin offering is not eaten, since perhaps they were not days of ziva, and this sin offering is non-sacred, and its pinching [melika] makes it a carcass, since non-sacred birds killed by pinching are nothing but a carcass. The burnt offering is sacrificed conditionally: if she is a zava, it is for her obligation, and if not, it is a gift offering. But there is no such thing as a gift sin offering.
rashi:b6.4: Except for “her petaḥ is seven” and “her petaḥ is eight,” who bring an offering and it is eaten: for whichever way you look at it, since she saw twelve consecutive days, they are zavot. Even if you say the first two were the end of ziva, it is still the beginning of niddah and ziva by the last count, for ten days remain to them, seven for niddah and three for flow; and all the more so if the first days were the beginning of niddah, or three of them were the end of ziva. Whichever way you look at it they are zavot. But all the earlier cases are possibly zavot: one can say three of those days were ziva and she is a zava, and one can say she is not a zava, since the first two days were of the end of ziva and by the last count she is no longer a zava.
rashi:b7.1: Is that to say that all to’ot are zavot? But this is a mere concern, and they are not certainly zavot.
rashi:b8.1: Rather, all zavot who are to’ot: implying all who can be treated as possibly zava because of her loss of count, that is, from “I saw three impure days” on.
rashi:b9.1: Mishna. There is no: purity in leprous marks in less than one week of quarantine.
rashi:b10.1: Gemara. Leprous marks of a person: they have [a quarantine of] one week, as written in the passage.
rashi:b10.2: Leprous marks of houses: three weeks, as taught in Torat Kohanim: “And the priest shall return” [Leviticus 14:39], “and the priest shall come” [14:44]: this is returning and this is coming. Just as with coming he removes [the stones], scrapes, plasters and gives it a week, so with returning, etc. And from where do we know that if the mark stayed as it was in both, in the first and the second week, he removes, scrapes, plasters and gives it a week, which is the third week? The verse states: “And the priest shall come,” “and if the priest shall come” [14:48]; what do we find, etc.
rashi:b11.1: These are leprous marks of a person: which are clarified within one week, whether to declare him pure or to confirm him [impure]; and this is a great kindness.
rashi:b12.1: If not for Your benevolence, etc.: as is explained below.
rashi:b13.1: With regard to what do they disagree, [etc.]; Rabbi Elazar says, He hides away: the Holy One, Blessed be He, hides away and conceals sins beneath the Throne of Glory, so that the merits outweigh.
rashi:b13.2: He lifts: He lifts and raises the pan of the sins upward, so that the merits outweigh.
rashi:b14.1: Rabba is in accordance with Rabbi Elazar: and this is what it means: “Your benevolence is like the mighty mountains,” in that You vindicate us by hiding away and concealing “Your judgments,” that is, the sins, in “the great deep.”
rashi:b14.2: And Rav Yehuda in accordance with Rabbi Yosei [son of Rabbi Ḥanina]: and this is what it means: “If not for Your benevolence like the mighty mountains,” which You do for us in lifting the sins, “who could stand before Your judgments,” which would weigh down to “the great deep”?
rashi:b15.1: Mishna. One does not decrease from four full months: of thirty days, in a year. Ulla explains the reason in the Gemara.
rashi:b15.2: Less than two: [not before] the second day from their baking.
rashi:b15.3: And not more than three: on the third day from their baking they are eaten, and no later. If the festival of Shavuot falls on Sunday, they are baked on Friday, since their baking overrides neither Shabbat nor a festival, and they are eaten on the festival after their waving, which is the third day. When Shavuot falls on one of the other days of the week, they are baked on the festival eve and eaten on the festival, which is the second day from their baking.
rashi:b15.4: The shewbread, etc.: how so? It is baked on Friday and eaten on the following Shabbat, which is the ninth day from its baking. If the two festival days of Rosh HaShana fell on Thursday and Friday, the shewbread is baked on Wednesday, arranged [on the Table] on Shabbat, and eaten on the second Shabbat, which is the eleventh day from its baking.
rashi:b16.1: A minor: is circumcised on the twelfth. How so? He was born at twilight on Friday. He is not circumcised on Shabbat, for perhaps it is the ninth day, since twilight is possibly day and possibly night, and if it was day, Shabbat turns out to be the ninth day; and circumcision not at its proper time overrides neither Shabbat nor a festival. And if the two festival days of Rosh HaShana fell after that Shabbat, he is not circumcised until Tuesday, which is the twelfth day from his birth.
rashi:b17.1: Gemara. It did not seem right to the Sages to make more than eight full, etc.: and the first clause of the mishna, which teaches, “one does not decrease from four full months,” means that we do not make more than eight deficient; but eight we do make. He does not explain it now; Ulla explains it below, and Rav Huna holds like Ulla.
rashi:b17.2: If so: if we make nine full months, the new moon would arrive three days before Rosh HaShana. For between this Tishrei’s molad and the next Tishrei’s molad there are four days, eight hours and 876 parts. If this Tishrei’s molad is at the beginning of Friday night, the next Tishrei’s molad falls eight hours into Wednesday. When we arrange the months one full and one deficient, Rosh HaShana is fixed on the day of the molad, for the order of the moon’s cycle is one full and one deficient: a lunar month is twenty-nine and a half days, two-thirds of an hour and 73 parts, so two months are 59 days, that is, one month of twenty-nine days and one of thirty. When we make seven full months, Rosh HaShana is pushed one day after the molad; if eight full, it is pushed two days; and if nine full, it is pushed three days.
tosafot:b9.1: And not more than three weeks: leprous marks of houses, for sometimes we do not know whether they are completely pure until three weeks; for example, if [the mark] stayed as it was in the first and in the second week, and he removed [the stones], scraped, plastered and gave it another week: if it returned, it requires demolition, and if it did not return, it is pure. But with a person we always know his status within two weeks, for if [the mark] stayed as it was in the second week he is pure at once; and in fewer days there is no knowing his purity, since there is no quarantine of less than seven.
tosafot:b11.1: “Your judgments are like the great deep”: leprous marks of houses, which can come to a delay of three weeks.
tosafot:b17.1: In brief: Tosafot first lay out the arithmetic. If last Tishrei’s molad was at the start of Friday night, this year’s is at 8 hours on Wednesday; with months alternating full and deficient, Rosh HaShana would be fixed on Wednesday, nine full months push the fixing three days to Shabbat, and “now, too,” eight full months put it on Friday, two days after the new moon is seen. They then report Rashi’s own difficulty: why not answer that sometimes the moon precedes by only one day, e.g., when last year’s molad was late on Wednesday, since the moon is hidden six hours and is not seen until the next day? Rashi’s commentary explains the Gemara’s leap-year answer this way (add 5 days, 21 hours, 589 parts; the molad falls on Thursday at 21 hours and, hidden six hours, is seen only on Friday night), and says that cases where eight full months still precede by two days (last year’s molad Friday at 18 hours) are no refutation, since the Gemara establishes the case where it precedes by only one. A further difficulty: the Gemara implies two days’ precedence never happens, yet today we postpone by the rule of GaTaRaD and fix on Thursday, two days later; one cannot say our practice simply differs from the Amoraim’s (as with the willow), since Rashi explained that we do not postpone from Shabbat for the shofar precisely to avoid two days. Rashi answered that GaTaRaD is not two days’ precedence, because for Babylonians the moon is hidden eighteen hours of the new (and six of the old), as at the end of the first chapter of Rosh HaShana (20b). Tosafot ask: then what was the Gemara’s difficulty, since a Wednesday molad at 8 hours, hidden eighteen hours, involves no two days? They answer that the Gemara took last year’s molad to be on Friday at 18 hours or later, the day before the fixing, parallel to the first clause as Ulla explains it, so that this year’s molad is Wednesday at 2 hours and is seen on Wednesday; which also explains why it did not answer that last year’s molad was on Shabbat at 10 hours. Lastly they ask how the opening objection, “it precedes by two days,” can stand when the molad might be at 9 hours and unseen all day, and answer that it objects where last year’s molad fell on the day before the fixing.
